full_judgment:
2. The opposite party No. 1 filed on 27th January, 1978 Pre-emption Case No. 16 of 1979 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in respect of certain land on the allegations, inter alia, that he was a co-sharer in the holding by inheritance and he had no knowledge about the transfer of the land under pre-emption to purchasers—the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, before me. The petitioners resisted the said case by filing joint written objection. Their case was that the case under section 96 of SAT Act was barred by limitation and they were benamder of his father Lal Mahmud who was a co-sharer in the holding in possession. 

 5. From perusal of the judgments of the courts below it appears that the pre-emption case was filed prior to the institution of the Title Suit by Lal Mahmud against the petitioners before me for declaration that they were his benamdcr and he was the real purchaser of the land under pre-emption. He obtained an ex parte decree in the suit in a hot haste on 7.12.78 within 3 months of its institution. But the pre-emption case although filed earlier was rejected on 20.7.82. In the case of Yakub Ali the pre-emption case was filed on 2.6.68 and the vendor of the land in that case contested the pre-emption case on the ground that there was an agreement for re-conveyance between him and the purchaser and he filed Title Suit No. 116 of 1966 on 15.6.67 for specific performance of contract and obtained an ex parte decree on 12.3.66. On facts the decision is distinguishable. In that case unlike the instant case there was an agreement for re-conveyance and the transfer was subject to that condition. Therefore, in my opinion, the principle laid down in that case has no manner of application to the facts in the present case. The learned Advocate also relied on the decision in the case of Balai Chandra Mondal Vs. Bibran Chandra Das 51 CWN 644 and the case of S Joga Moya Debi and others Vs. SDD Singh Hazari 36 DLR 272 in support of his contention that in a pre-emption case the court cannot examine the benami nature of transaction. He also cited the case of Upendra Vs. Janab Ali, 29 DLR 229. None of the cases cited has relevancy to the instant case. From the judgment impugned before me it appears that the learned Judge while allowing the Miscellaneous Case found that the Title Suit No. 159 of 1978 was filed after 7 months of filing the pre-emption case and plaintiff, Lal Mahmud obtained the ex parte decree against the party Nos. 1 and 2 within 3 months of the institution of the suit, that appellant before him was not impleaded in the title suit as a party to whom a statutory right of pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act accrues and the decree was a collusive one and was not binding upon the opposite party No. 1 pre-emptor. Thus, it appears that the lower appellate Court did not enter into the question of benami transaction; rather it proceeded on the ground that the ex parte decree passed in the Title Suit was obtained collusively without impleading the pre-emptor in the suit although the pre-emption case was filed earlier to the institution of the Title Suit. The contention that as at the time of disposal of the pre-emption case there being no subsisting title to the pre-emptees under the kabala in view of the decree made in the Title Suit instituted by Lal Mahmud the pre-emption case is not maintainable is misconceived as it has been found and, according to me correctly, by the appellate Court that the decree made in Title Suit is not binding upon the pre-emptor as he was not made party to the said Title Suit. Where during pendency of a pre-emption case under section 96 of the SAT Act a decree is passed in a suit where the pre-emptor is not impleaded as party the decree made in that suit does not defeat the right of the pre-emptor accrued to him under section 96 of the SAT Act to pre-empt the land. The decision in the case of Meher Abjar Vs. Jalal Ahmed Howlader, 13 DLR 642 supports this view of mine. In the instant case the appellate Court did not proceed to examine the question of benami and as such the decisions cited in this case on behalf of the petitioners have no manner of application.
